children: Saudi Arabia is pumping 5.8M bbl/day—more than 80% of capacity—through its key East-West oil pipeline, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said Tuesday, in a fresh sign of recovering export capacity out of the Middle East.

The 750-mile pipeline, which has a capacity of ~7M bbl/day, was forced to shut down on September 11 after drone attacks and halted crude loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu, but it restarted operations within 5-6 days of the attacks, the minister said at the Made in GCC 2026 Forum and Exhibition in Bahrain.

Middle Eastern crude flows are indeed improving, with shipping data showing regional exports exceeding pre-war levels on some days in late September as producers used alternative routes and logistical adjustments to keep barrels moving, Priyanka Sachdeva at Phillip Nova said in a note.

However, renewed attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz mean that while barrels are still moving, the cost, insurance, routing, and security risks of moving them remain elevated, Sachdeva said.

U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said a tanker entering the Strait of Hormuz on Monday was hailed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps offshore Oman and instructed to turn back or risk being targeted; the vessel complied.

Further, the recovery is uneven across the oil market; the seven-day average for crude shipments through Hormuz reached 10.3M bbl/day as of October 3, or 76% of pre-war levels, according to Kpler data cited by

, but refined products such as diesel and gasoline totaled 1.3M bbl/day, accounting for only 11% of overall flows through the strait, down from more than 20% before the war, as damage to Middle Eastern refineries continued to constrain fuel supplies.
